        self.play(Create(dist_curve), run_time=2)

        lecture_lines = [
            "Let's pick random groups of thirty creatures each.",
            "Calculate each group's average height and record it.",

            sample_creatures.animate.set_color(color_1).scale(1.4),

        # Perform several visible iterations

            # Logic: Select new random group, show them briefly, drop ball
            new_indices = random.sample(range(len(population)), 30)
            new_sample = VGroup(*[population[idx] for idx in new_indices])
            
            # Reset visual of previously used dots (if any were the same)
            # and highlight new ones
            val = random.gauss(5, 0.6)
            t_pos = sampling_axis.n2p(val)
            
            # Move dots back to normal and hide color for others
            # But simpler: just flash the new sample
            m_ball = Dot(radius=0.08, color=color_3)
            m_ball.move_to(new_sample.get_center())
            
            self.play(
                new_sample.animate(run_time=0.2).set_color(color_3),
                FadeIn(m_ball, run_time=0.1)
            )
            self.play(
                m_ball.animate(run_time=0.3).move_to(t_pos),
                new_sample.animate(run_time=0.2).set_color(GRAY_C)

        )

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Initial Setup
        title = "The Emergence of the Bell Curve"
        lines = [
            'Watch the chaotic forest distribution begin to fade.',
            'A new, smooth shape grows from our recorded averages.',
            'Surprisingly, a perfect bell curve emerges from the chaos.',
            'This transformation happens regardless of the original distribution.'
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Setup Axes and Distributions
        # Upper area (A1-B6) for original distribution
        # Lower area (D1-F6) for the new histogram/curve
        
        # --- Upper Bimodal Distribution ---
        def bimodal_func(x):
            # Sum of two Gaussians
            return 1.5 * (np.exp(-((x - 1)**2) / 0.4) + np.exp(-((x + 1)**2) / 0.4))

        upper_axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 2],
            axis_config={"include_tip": False},
            x_length=4.5, y_length=1.5
        ).set_color(WHITE)
        bimodal_curve = upper_axes.plot(bimodal_func, color=WHITE)
        bimodal_group = VGroup(upper_axes, bimodal_curve)
        self.place_in_area(bimodal_group, "A1", "B6")

        # --- Lower Histogram Axes ---
        lower_axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 10],
            axis_config={"include_tip": False},
            x_length=4.5, y_length=2.5
        ).set_color(WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(lower_axes, "D1", "F6")
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Fade out original distribution to #333333
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#333333")
        self.add(bimodal_group)
        self.play(
            bimodal_group.animate.set_color("#333333"),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Rapidly drop 500 sample mean balls
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        
        # We'll simulate 500 balls by creating stacks in bins
        num_bins = 20
        bin_edges = np.linspace(-2.5, 2.5, num_bins + 1)
        bin_centers = (bin_edges[:-1] + bin_edges[1:]) / 2
        
        # Standard deviation for the normal curve we're building
        mu, sigma = 0, 0.8
        
        # Calculate counts for each bin to form a normal distribution
        # Total balls = 500
        total_balls = 500
        probs = np.exp(-0.5 * ((bin_centers - mu) / sigma)**2)
        probs /= probs.sum()
        bin_counts = (probs * total_balls).astype(int)

        all_balls = VGroup()
        ball_radius = 0.04
        
        # Prepare the dots (balls)
        for i, count in enumerate(bin_counts):
            x_val = lower_axes.c2p(bin_centers[i], 0)[0]
            base_y = lower_axes.c2p(0, 0)[1]
            for j in range(count):
                dot = Dot(radius=ball_radius, color=WHITE)
                dot.move_to([x_val, base_y + j * (ball_radius * 2.2), 0])
                all_balls.add(dot)

        # Animate dropping balls in batches to stay within runtime but look "rapid"
        batch_size = 25
        batches = [all_balls[i:i + batch_size] for i in range(0, len(all_balls), batch_size)]
        
        self.add(lower_axes)
        for batch in batches:
            self.play(
                FadeIn(batch, shift=UP*0.5),
                run_time=0.1
            )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Transition to Bell-shaped outline (Color #00FF00)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FF00")
        
        # Highlight balls to green
        self.play(
            all_balls.animate.set_color("#00FF00"),
            run_time=1
        )
        
        # Draw a green outline (histogram-like)
        hist_outline = lower_axes.plot(
            lambda x: 9 * np.exp(-0.5 * (x / 0.8)**2),
            color="#00FF00",
            x_range=[-2.5, 2.5]
        )
        self.play(Create(hist_outline), run_time=1.5)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Draw a smooth mathematical curve (Color: #1E90FF)
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#1E90FF")
        
        # Smooth curve
        normal_curve = lower_axes.plot(
            lambda x: 9 * np.exp(-0.5 * (x / 0.8)**2),
            color="#1E90FF",
            stroke_width=6
        )
        curve_label = Text("Normal Distribution", color="#1E90FF", font_size=24)
        # Position label near the peak
        self.place_at_grid(curve_label, "D3", scale_factor=1.0)
        curve_label.shift(UP*0.5)

        self.play(
            Create(normal_curve),
            Write(curve_label),
            run_time=2
        )
        
        # Flash the curve
        self.play(Flash(normal_curve, color="#1E90FF", line_length=0.4, num_lines=15), run_time=1)
        self.wait(2)

sections.title: The Mystery of Predictability
sections.content: Introduce the paradox: while individual events are unpredictable, their collective averages follow a strict pattern. Hook the audience by showing a variety of chaotic, non-normal distributions (flat, skewed, or spiked).
sections.example: Imagine a 'Fairytale Forest' where some creatures are tiny (10cm) and some are giants (500cm), with almost nothing in between. Their individual heights are a chaotic 'Bimodal' distribution.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Histogram and the Mean
sections.content: Quickly review the basics: A Histogram shows frequency, and the Mean (average) is the balancing point. Explain that we aren't looking at individual data points, but at 'Sample Means'.
sections.example: Visualizing a bar chart of the heights of 1,000 individual forest creatures. It looks like two separate towers far apart, not a bell.

sections.title: The Sampling Experiment
sections.content: Introduce the process of sampling. Explain that we take a small group (size n), calculate their average, and record it. Repeat this process hundreds of times. Emphasize that the size of 'n' is the secret lever.
sections.example: A group of 30 creatures is randomly picked from the forest. We calculate their average height and drop a ball into a new graph. We repeat this 500 times.

sections.title: The Emergence of the Bell Curve
sections.content: Show the transformation visually. As the number of samples increases, the histogram of the 'Sample Means' begins to morph into a symmetrical, bell-shaped curve (Normal Distribution), regardless of the original forest distribution's shape.
sections.example: Animation: The two towers of the forest creatures' heights fade, and a new, smooth, blue 'Bell Curve' (Gaussian distribution) grows from the falling sample balls.

sections.title: Defining the Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
sections.content: Formalize the concept: 1. The sampling distribution of the mean will be nearly normal. 2. This happens if the sample size (n) is large enough (usually n > 30). 3. The center of this bell is the true population mean.
sections.example: Mathematical Overlay: Show the formula [x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n)] using glowing icons where 'n' (sample size) clearly shows that as it gets bigger, the bell gets narrower and more accurate.

sections.title: Real-World Power: Why It Matters
sections.content: Explain that because of CLT, we can use the Normal Distribution to make predictions about almost anything (heights, test scores, error rates) even if we don't know the original population's shape.
sections.example: A quality control robot in a factory measuring the 'fizz level' in soda cans. It doesn't need to check every can; by checking small batches, it can predict the quality of the entire million-can run using the Bell Curve.

sections.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
sections.content: Summarize: Chaos at the micro-level leads to perfect Normal Distribution at the macro-level. The CLT is the bridge between individual uncertainty and statistical certainty.
sections.example: Final visual: A chaotic swarm of individual dots at the bottom of the screen funneling upward into a perfectly glowing, stable Bell Curve at the top.
